content: Beclomethasone dipropionate (BDP) is available in a variety of daily doses for the management of chronic asthma. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether there is a dose-response relationship for BDP in the treatment of long-term asthma. To gather relevant data, researchers conducted a comprehensive search using the Cochrane Airways Group trial register, the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, and reference lists from related articles. They also contacted study authors and Glaxo Wellcome UK to identify eligible studies. Additionally, proceedings from respiratory society meetings and journals such as the British Journal of Clinical Research and the European Journal of Clinical Research were manually searched for relevant studies. The inclusion criteria required prospective, randomized trials that compared two or more daily doses of BDP in patients aged two years or older with chronic asthma. Two reviewers independently assessed the quality of the studies, and data extraction was performed by one reviewer. Study authors were contacted to clarify study designs and obtain missing data. A total of 15 trials were included in the analysis. The methodological quality of these studies varied, and many did not clearly describe the baseline level of asthma control in participants. The studies evaluated dose differences ranging from less than two-fold to five-fold. The results were reported as weighted mean differences (WMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and the number of trials contributing to each outcome was specified. In patients with asthma who were not treated with oral steroids, a small benefit was observed with a daily dose of 800 mcg of BDP compared to 400 mcg. Specifically, there was an improvement in morning peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) by 11 L/min (95% CI: 4 to 19 L/min) based on two trials. Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) improved by 9 ml (95% CI: 3 to 140 ml) in one trial. Night-time symptom scores also showed a reduction, with a WMD of 0.13 (95% CI: 0.04 to 0.22) in one trial. Studies comparing 1000 mcg versus 500 mcg and 1600 mcg versus 400 mcg of BDP demonstrated a significant advantage of higher doses in terms of histamine bronchial hyper-responsiveness (BHR) and percentage improvement in FEV1 from baseline. However, no differences were observed between higher and lower doses of BDP for outcomes such as daytime symptoms, withdrawal rates due to asthma exacerbations, oropharyngeal side effects, or measures of hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis function. Additionally, in patients dependent on oral corticosteroids (OCS), there was no significant difference in the prednisolone-sparing effect between high and low doses of BDP. In conclusion, BDP exhibits a shallow dose-response effect for a limited number of efficacy outcomes across daily doses ranging from 400 mcg to 1600 mcg in the treatment of long-term asthma. However, the clinical relevance of the improvements observed with higher doses remains uncertain.
